The parameters of a model are the numbers in it: transmission rates, durations, shares, and the like. This page covers where they live, their units, how to name them so they can be documented, changed, and fitted, and the forms a value can take: a number, a value for each group, a value that changes over time, or one that varies between people.

## Values live in the model

In a declared disease, a value lives where it is used. There is no separate block of parameters to fill in: each number becomes a parameter, named after its role:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.pars
```

The number that multiplies a source of infection is `beta` (named by its transition, `beta_infection`, only where two would have the same name). A duration is named by the state it is the time in (`dur_E`, `dur_I`), or by its transition if people can leave that state after more than one duration (`dur_recovery`, `dur_death`), and a rate by its transition (`rate_death`). What a number means is given by where it is: after `@` and multiplying `I`, a rate; as `init_prev=`, a share of the population.

## Units of time

A typed value says its unit: `ss.days(8)` is a duration, and `ss.perday(1.9)`, `ss.peryear(0.02)` are rates. A bare number takes the unit of the model, which is the unit of its typed values: here days, from `ss.days(8)`, so β = 1.9 is per day. The rates of births and deaths don't count, so adding births per year to this model leaves β per day. A model whose other typed values are in different units (a duration in days and another in years) has no single unit for its bare numbers, which is an error that asks for `unit=`; giving every rate a type avoids it.

Values are converted to the time step of the sim, whatever it is, so the same model can be run with a step of a day or a week. A rate (`ss.perday`) is a rate, converted exactly. A probability over a period, such as a 10% chance of recovering each day, is written `ss.prob(0.1, 'day')`, and is converted as a probability: over a week it is 1 − 0.9^7, not 0.7. See [Time](building_time.qmd) for durations, rates, and dates.

## Named parameters

When a parameter is to be documented, reused, or fitted, give it a name with `ss.par()`. It behaves like its value in a rate, so it can be used anywhere a number can:

```{python}
beta = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day', source='Chosen to give R0 of about 15')
dur  = ss.par(ss.days(8), bounds=[ss.days(6), ss.days(10)], doc='Infectious period', source='About 4 days either side of the rash')

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ dur
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.pars
```

- The name is taken from the variable (`beta`), or given with `name=`.
- `bounds` is the range of plausible values. A parameter with bounds can be fitted: `sim.fit()` fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data ([Fitting a model](calibration_fitting.qmd)). A value outside its bounds is an error.
- `doc` (what it means) and `source` (where the value came from) are free text. `describe()` shows them under the transition that uses the parameter, and they are kept when the model is saved.
- `prior=` gives a distribution of belief about the value, used only in calibration ([Gradients](calibration_gradients.qmd)).
- `label=` is a human-readable name, for plots and tables.

For a disease that makes its states and transitions in `__init__()` (see [Declaring in `__init__()`](building_diseases.qmd#declaring-in-__init__)), `ss.pars(defaults, **kwargs)` makes several named parameters at once from a dict of defaults and the values given, as a class body's `ss.par()` lines would; see [`ss.pars`](../api/transitions.qmd). [Appendix: how a number is named](#appendix-how-a-number-is-named) lists the names Starsim gives numbers that aren't named.

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.describe()
```

## Changing a parameter

A parameter can be changed when the sim is made, by name, without changing the model. This is how a set of values for one setting, or a fitted set, is used:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.5), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
print('R0 with beta = 1.5:', round(sim.diseases.measles.R0(), 1))
```

With several modules, a parameter's name is given with its module's, e.g. `pars={'measles.beta': 1.5}`. A name that matches no parameter is an error, which lists the names there are, so a misspelled parameter is never silently ignored:

```{python}
try:
    ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(betta=1.5)).init()
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)
```

A parameter can also be changed during a run, from a date or when a condition holds, with `ss.modify()`; see [Interventions](interventions_interventions.qmd).

## The forms a value can take

Where a value is given decides what it means; the form it takes is free. Each of these can be a rate, a duration, a share, or a starting value:

| Form | Example | Means |
|---|---|---|
| A number | `1.9` | The same for everyone, always (in the model's unit of time) |
| A typed value | `ss.perday(1.9)`, `ss.days(8)` | The same, in its own unit |
| A value for each group | `ss.by(age=[2.5, 1.9, 1.0])` | One value for each age group (or other group) |
| A time series | `ss.timeseries({'2025-01-01': 1.9, '2025-03-01': 1.2})` | Changes over time, from given values |
| A seasonal cycle | `ss.seasonal(mean=1.9, amplitude=0.2, peak='March')` | A yearly cycle around a mean |
| A function of the sim | `lambda sim: 1.9 if sim.now < ss.date('2025-03-01') else 1.2` | Worked out at each step |
| A distribution | `ss.lognormal(mean=ss.days(8), std=ss.days(2))` | Varies between people |
| A function of the sim and the people | `lambda sim, uids: ...` | One value for each person (agents only) |

A function takes any of `self` (the module whose value it is), `sim`, and `uids` (the people it is for), by those names, in any order: `lambda sim: ...`, `lambda self, sim: ...`, and `lambda self, sim, uids: ...` all work. One that takes `uids` gives a value for each person, so runs as agents only; one that doesn't means the same under every solver.

Any of these can be wrapped in `ss.par()` to give it a name, bounds, or a source. The sections below cover each kind.

### Values for each group

`ss.by()` gives a value for each level of a stratification. Here, in a town where 80% of children (0–14), 92% of adults (15–64), and 98% of older adults (65+) are immune, susceptible children are the most likely to be infected, and older adults the least, as a higher β for children than for older adults says. Each scenario reports the share of each group's susceptible people who are infected over a year:

```{python}
import pandas as pd

def make_measles(beta):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share in each
    return measles

betas = {
    'The same for everyone': 1.9,
    'By age':                ss.by(age=[2.5, 1.9, 1.0]),
}
attack = {}
for label, beta in betas.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(beta), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    res = sim.results.measles
    attack[label] = {age: round(res.infection.select(age=age).sum() / res.S.select(age=age)[0], 2) for age in ['0-14', '15-64', '65+']}
pd.DataFrame(attack) # The share of each group's susceptible people infected
```

With the same β for everyone and homogeneous mixing, every susceptible person has the same risk, so the same share of each group is infected (about two-thirds), whatever its size or immunity. With β by age, the share is higher among children and lower among older adults; since children are most of those still susceptible, the outbreak as a whole is also larger.

Here the values are per day, and mixing is homogeneous, so a higher β means a higher rate of infection for susceptible people in that group. The values can also be given by label (`ss.by(age={'0-14': 2.5, ...})`), as a table, or for several dimensions at once. See [Stratification](building_stratification.qmd#values-by-group). They can also come from code, as a function of the sim that gives one value per level, worked out at each step: `ss.by(patch=fn)`, e.g. a biting rate in each place from mosquitoes written as code, whatever other dimensions the sim has.

### Values that change over time

Contact patterns, reporting, and treatment change over time, and so do the parameters that stand for them. A value can be a time series (`ss.timeseries()`), held or interpolated between given dates; a smooth yearly cycle (`ss.seasonal()`); or a function of the sim, worked out at each step. Each goes wherever a number would, in a rate, a share, or a starting value. [Time](building_time.qmd#values-that-change-over-time) covers them, with examples of measles with and without school terms. A change made by an intervention, from a date or when a condition holds (`ss.modify()`), is covered in [Interventions](interventions_interventions.qmd).

## Values that vary between people

A distribution, given as a value, gives each person their own value: `recovery = I >> R @ ss.lognormal(mean=ss.days(8), std=ss.days(2))` gives each person their own infectious period. For durations, a compartmental run represents the distribution with stages; see [Durations](building_diseases.qmd#durations) and [Distributions](mechanics_distributions.qmd).

A function of the sim and the people, `fn(sim, uids)`, returns one value for each person it is given, and can use anything about them. Here the infectious period is longer for children under 5 (a made-up example):

```{python}
def dur_fn(sim, uids):
    age = sim.people.age[uids]
    return ss.days(8 + 4*(age < 5)) # 12 days for children under 5, 8 for everyone else

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.constant(dur_fn)) # Each person's own duration, as given
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
same = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.constant(ss.days(8))), init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

pars = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(30), dt=ss.days(0.25), verbose=0) # A quarter-day step, short enough for measles as agents
msim = ss.parallel({
    '8 days for everyone': ss.Sim(same, **pars),
    '12 days under 5':     ss.Sim(measles, **pars),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

Nearly everyone is infected in the first week or two either way, but with the longer infectious period of young children, the last of them stay infectious for days longer, so the tail of the epidemic is longer. Children under 5 are only a few percent of the population, so the effect is only as large as the group the function applies to.

A rate is worked out for the people who could take it at each step (everyone in its source state), so a function in a rate is called for them, every step. Multiplied by a condition, it is called only for the people the condition holds for, and is 0 for the others: with `rate = ss.par(fn, name='infant')*(ss.person.age < 1)`, `fn` is given only the children under 1, and need not check their ages itself.

A function that uses `uids`, or anything else about individual people, needs agents, so a model with one runs as agents. Where the same thing can be said by group (`ss.by(age=...)` on a stratified model), it runs under every solver.

A distribution in a rate gives each person their own rate: in `S >> I @ ss.gamma(a=0.5, scale=3.8)*I`, each person has their own transmission rate (the same as `ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.gamma(a=0.5, scale=3.8)*I)`). A distribution on its own after `@` is a dwell time; times a state, it is a rate.

## Parameters of modules written as code

A module written as code (see [Custom modules](building_modules.qmd)) declares its parameters, and their defaults, in its `__init__()` with `self.define_pars()`, and then takes the values it was given with `self.update_pars()`:

```{python}
class Antibodies(ss.Module):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            half_life = ss.days(60), # How quickly antibodies decline
            boost     = 1.0,         # The antibody level just after recovery
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)

antibodies = Antibodies(half_life=ss.days(90))
print(antibodies.pars)
```

The point of `define_pars()` is to set the ground truth for what each parameter is. The values given to the module are checked against it, so a misspelled name is an error:

```{python}
try:
    Antibodies(half_lfe=ss.days(90))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)
```

A value can be given in any form that fits the default. For a parameter whose default is a distribution, a number sets the distribution's main value, and another distribution replaces it. For example, in the library's SIR written as code (`ssl.AgentSIR`), the chance of death is a Bernoulli distribution (a yes or no for each person), so it can be given as a probability or as another Bernoulli distribution, but not as a distribution of another kind, since what the module does with it (picking who dies) needs a yes or no:

```{python}
import starsim.library as ssl

print(ssl.AgentSIR(p_death=0.02).pars.p_death)                  # A probability: the p of the default
print(ssl.AgentSIR(p_death=ss.bernoulli(p=0.2)).pars.p_death)   # Another Bernoulli distribution
print(ssl.AgentSIR(dur_inf=ss.gamma(a=4, scale=ss.days(2.5))).pars.dur_inf) # Any distribution of durations: here a mean of 10 days
try:
    ssl.AgentSIR(p_death=ss.lognormal(4))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)
```

A parameter of a distribution can itself be a function of the sim and the people it is drawn for, which is how a module written as code makes a value depend on age, sex, or anything else the sim knows; see [Distributions](mechanics_distributions.qmd).

## Pitfalls

- **A bare number in the wrong unit.** A bare number is in the model's unit of time: in a model whose unit is years, `I >> R @ 0.125` is 0.125 per year. Typed values (`ss.perday(0.125)`, `ss.days(8)`) don't depend on it.
- **Changing the model instead of the sim.** To try another value, give it to the sim (`pars=dict(beta=1.5)`) rather than changing the disease, which every sim made from it shares.
- **A distribution as a value or as a prior.** A distribution as a value is variation between people. Uncertainty about a single value is a prior, `ss.par(1.9, prior=...)`, used only in calibration.
- **A function where a time series would do.** A function can't be printed by `describe()`, exported to another framework, or written out as equations.

## Further reading

- [epiparameter](https://epiverse-trace.github.io/epiparameter/): a library of epidemiological parameters (incubation periods, serial intervals, and the like) from the literature, in R
- [Rates and probabilities in economic modelling](https://doi.org/10.2165/00019053-200725010-00002): converting between rates and probabilities over different periods
- [pomp](https://kingaa.github.io/pomp/): estimating the parameters of stochastic dynamic models, in R

## Appendix: how a number is named

A number written in a declared disease becomes a parameter, named by where it is, so that it can be given by name (`pars=dict(...)`) and fitted. These are the rules:

| Where the number is | Its name |
|---|---|
| Multiplying a source of infection (`1.9*I`) | `beta`, or `beta_<transition>` if the disease has more than one transmission |
| A duration, the only way out of its state | `dur_<state>` (e.g. `dur_I`) |
| A duration of a transition out of a state with several ways out | `dur_<transition>` (e.g. `dur_death`) |
| Any other rate (`ss.perday(0.001)`, `ss.prob(0.01, 'week')`) | `rate_<transition>` |
| The share of a separate transition, `p=` | `p_<transition>` |
| `init_prev=` | `init_prev` |
| Anything else inline: a factor such as the 0.5 in `0.5*A`, a list of shares for one transition's destinations, starting values in `init=`, an outcome's share or delay | Not a parameter; wrap it in `ss.par()` to make it one |

A parameter made with `ss.par()` keeps its own name (from the variable, or `name=`). To see the names in a model, print its parameters:

```{python}
S, E, I, A, R = ss.states('S E I A R')
example = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> E @ 0.5*(I + 0.5*A),                    # beta (the 0.5 on A is not a parameter)
    onset     = ss.Transition(E, [I, A], p=[0.6, 0.4], dur=ss.days(5)), # dur_E (the shares are not parameters)
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(7), p=0.99), # dur_recovery and p_recovery, since I has two ways out
    death     = ss.Transition(I, ss.dead, dur=ss.days(9), p=0.01),
    clear     = A >> R @ ss.days(5),                         # dur_A
    waning    = R >> S @ ss.prob(0.01, 'week'),              # rate_waning
    init_prev = 0.001,
)
example.pars
```
